title: Kubernetes RBAC
summary: Kubernetes RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) controls who can do what on which resources in the cluster. Every kubectl command is an HTTP request — RBAC decides if that request is allowed. Misconfigured RBAC is one of the most common Kubernetes security failures: pods with cluster-admin ServiceAccounts, users with wildcard permissions, or no RBAC at all.

sections.title: RBAC building blocks: Subjects, Verbs, Resources
sections.body:
## Role-Based Access Control: the authorization layer for everything in Kubernetes

Every interaction with a Kubernetes cluster — whether from `kubectl`, a CI/CD pipeline, an operator controller, or a pod calling the API — is an HTTP request to the API server. **RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)** is the gatekeeper that decides whether each request is allowed or denied. Without it, any process that can reach the API server can read secrets, delete deployments, or modify cluster configuration.

RBAC is built on a simple three-part question: **Who** is making the request? **What** action are they trying to take? **On which resource?** The "who" is called a **subject** — it can be a human user (whose identity comes from an X.509 certificate or an OIDC token), a group, or a **ServiceAccount** (a namespaced Kubernetes object that provides an identity for processes running inside pods). Every pod runs under a ServiceAccount; if you don't specify one, Kubernetes uses the `default` ServiceAccount in its namespace.

The "what" is expressed as an HTTP **verb**: `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`, and `deletecollection` map to standard CRUD operations. Some resources also have **subresources** — `pods/exec` controls whether you can run `kubectl exec`, `pods/log` controls `kubectl logs`. Granting `pods/exec` is effectively granting shell access to every pod that matches the selector, which is why it must be treated with the same seriousness as granting SSH access.

The "on which resource" combines the **API group** (e.g., `apps` for Deployments, `""` for core resources like Pods and Secrets), the **resource type**, and optionally a specific **resource name**. This three-dimensional model — subject × verb × resource — is what makes fine-grained least-privilege access control possible in Kubernetes.

**Every action in Kubernetes is an HTTP verb on a resource:**

```
kubectl get pods           → GET    /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods
kubectl delete deployment  → DELETE /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments/my-app
kubectl apply -f           → PATCH or CREATE depending on existence
```

**RBAC answers the question:** "Is `{subject}` allowed to perform `{verb}` on `{resource}` in `{namespace}`?"

**Subjects — who is making the request:**

```
User            — human (e.g., "alice@company.com")
                  Kubernetes has no User objects; identity comes from x.509 certs or OIDC

Group           — a set of users (e.g., "devops-team")
                  Assigned by the authentication provider (OIDC groups, cert CN)

ServiceAccount  — identity for pods (processes running inside the cluster)
                  Created as an object: kubectl create serviceaccount my-app
                  Automatically mounted into pods at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
```

**Verbs — what action:**

```
get       — read a single resource
list      — read a collection
watch     — stream updates (used by controllers)
create    — create a new resource
update    — replace a resource
patch     — partially update a resource
delete    — delete a resource
deletecollection — delete multiple resources

# Special verbs:
use       — for PodSecurityPolicy / StorageClass
bind      — for RoleBindings
escalate  — create a Role with more permissions than you have
impersonate — act as another user
```

**Resources — what Kubernetes object type:**

```bash
# List all available resources and their API groups
kubectl api-resources

# Common resources:
pods                       — core API group (v1)
deployments                — apps/v1
services                   — v1
secrets                    — v1
configmaps                 — v1
namespaces                 — v1 (cluster-scoped)
nodes                      — v1 (cluster-scoped)
clusterroles               — rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
rolebindings               — rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
```

**Subresources** — actions on a sub-endpoint:

```
pods/log      — kubectl logs
pods/exec     — kubectl exec
pods/portforward — kubectl port-forward
deployments/scale — kubectl scale

# Granting exec is a BIG DEAL — it's essentially shell access to the pod:
# rules:
# - apiGroups: [""]
#   resources: ["pods/exec"]    # Never grant this in production without careful thought
#   verbs: ["create"]
```

sections.title: Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings
sections.body:
## Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings: the four RBAC objects

Kubernetes RBAC uses exactly four object types, and understanding the distinction between them is essential before writing any RBAC configuration.

A **Role** is a set of permission rules that applies within a single **namespace**. It can only grant access to namespace-scoped resources (Pods, Services, Deployments, Secrets, ConfigMaps) within that namespace. A Role in the `production` namespace cannot grant access to anything in `staging`.

A **ClusterRole** has two distinct uses. First, it can grant access to **cluster-scoped resources** that have no namespace — Nodes, PersistentVolumes, Namespaces, and ClusterRoles themselves. Second, a ClusterRole can be used as a *template* and bound within a specific namespace via a `RoleBinding`. This lets you define a reusable permission set once (e.g., "pod reader") and bind it in multiple namespaces without duplicating the Role definition.

A **RoleBinding** grants a Role or ClusterRole to one or more subjects **within a specific namespace**. Even if you bind a ClusterRole via a RoleBinding, the resulting permissions are scoped to that namespace only.

A **ClusterRoleBinding** grants a ClusterRole to subjects **across the entire cluster** — all namespaces. This is appropriate for cluster-wide operators (like Prometheus needing to scrape metrics from every namespace) but should be used sparingly. Most application workloads should use namespace-scoped Role + RoleBinding.

Kubernetes ships with four built-in ClusterRoles worth knowing: `cluster-admin` (full access — treat as break-glass only), `admin` (full namespace access minus modifying the namespace itself), `edit` (read/write most resources, no RBAC objects), and `view` (read-only). Prefer these as starting points and scope them down rather than inventing roles from scratch.

**Four RBAC objects:**

```
Role            — permissions within ONE namespace
ClusterRole     — permissions cluster-wide OR reusable namespace role template
RoleBinding     — grants a Role or ClusterRole to a Subject within a namespace
ClusterRoleBinding — grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide
```

**Role — namespace-scoped:**

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]           # "" = core API group (pods, services, configmaps)
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
```

**ClusterRole — applies across all namespaces:**

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["metrics.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["nodes", "pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
```

**RoleBinding — grants a role to a subject in one namespace:**

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: alice-pod-reader
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice@company.com
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app
  namespace: production          # ServiceAccount namespace must match
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader               # must exist in same namespace
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**ClusterRoleBinding — grants a ClusterRole across all namespaces:**

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: monitoring-reader
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: prometheus
  namespace: monitoring
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**Built-in ClusterRoles (use these as starting points):**

```
cluster-admin  — full access to everything (use only for break-glass)
admin          — full namespace access (cannot modify the namespace itself)
edit           — read/write most resources (no roles/rolebindings)
view           — read-only on most resources

# Check what a built-in role allows:
kubectl describe clusterrole view
```

sections.title: Production RBAC patterns
sections.body:
## Least privilege in practice: patterns for real-world RBAC

The **principle of least privilege** is the single most important idea in access control: every subject should have exactly the permissions needed to perform its function — no more, no less. In Kubernetes, violating this principle is surprisingly easy because the path of least resistance is often to grant broad access ("just use `cluster-admin`") and the consequences are deferred until a security incident.

The most dangerous RBAC misconfiguration in the wild is giving application pods a ServiceAccount bound to `cluster-admin`. If any such pod is compromised — through a dependency vulnerability, an RCE bug, or a supply chain attack — the attacker inherits full cluster control: they can read all secrets across all namespaces, create privileged pods to escape to the node, and exfiltrate or destroy everything. A properly scoped ServiceAccount limits the blast radius to what that specific pod legitimately needs.

**ServiceAccount token auto-mounting** is a subtle default that compounds this risk. Kubernetes automatically mounts the ServiceAccount's API token into every pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`. If your application doesn't call the Kubernetes API, this token is unnecessary attack surface — setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount removes it.

For **CI/CD pipelines**, the deploy-bot pattern is the right model: the pipeline's ServiceAccount or kubeconfig can update Deployments and ConfigMaps but cannot touch Secrets, RBAC objects, or cluster-scoped resources. This means a compromised CI system cannot escalate to full cluster access.

ArgoCD adds its own RBAC layer on top of Kubernetes RBAC — controlling which users and groups can sync, delete, or view which ArgoCD Applications — using a ConfigMap-based policy language. Both layers must be correctly configured in a GitOps setup.

**Principle of least privilege — never grant more than needed:**

```yaml
# Bad: app has cluster-admin (seen in the wild far too often)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: my-app
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: my-app-admin
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin     # ← if this pod is compromised, attacker owns the cluster
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**Correct pattern: scope to what the app actually needs:**

```yaml
# Good: app only reads secrets in its own namespace
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: secret-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  resourceNames: ["db-credentials", "api-key"]  # even specific which secrets!
  verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: my-app-secret-reader
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app
  namespace: production
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: secret-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**Disable automounting for sensitive service accounts:**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: production
automountServiceAccountToken: false   # opt-out of auto-mounting the token

# Or per-pod:
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
```

**CI/CD pipeline RBAC (deploy-bot pattern):**

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: deploy-bot
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "daemonsets", "statefulsets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: [""]    
  resources: ["services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update", "patch"]
# Note: no delete, no RBAC objects, no secrets
```

**ArgoCD RBAC (its own RBAC layer on top of Kubernetes RBAC):**

```yaml
# argocd-rbac-cm ConfigMap
data:
  policy.csv: |
    # Format: p, subject, resource, action, object, allow/deny
    p, role:developer, applications, get, */*, allow
    p, role:developer, applications, sync, */*, allow
    p, role:developer, applications, delete, */*, deny
    g, devops-team, role:admin
    g, dev-team, role:developer
  policy.default: role:readonly
```

sections.title: Auditing and debugging RBAC
sections.body:
## Debugging RBAC: a systematic approach

RBAC misconfigurations produce cryptic 403 Forbidden errors that can be difficult to diagnose without the right tools. The good news is Kubernetes provides a first-class debugging verb: `kubectl auth can-i`.

The `--as` flag is the key to debugging access for another subject without actually logging in as that subject. You can impersonate any user, group, or ServiceAccount to ask "would this request be allowed?" — a capability called **subject access review** (SAR). This is how you verify that a new Role actually grants what you intended, and that it doesn't accidentally grant more.

When diagnosing a 403, the systematic approach is: identify the exact subject (user or ServiceAccount), identify the exact verb and resource from the error message, use `kubectl auth can-i` to confirm the denial, then inspect all RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings that reference that subject to understand what *is* granted. Tools like `kubectl auth can-i --list` give you the full permission matrix for a subject.

**Kubernetes audit logs** are the authoritative record of every API request — who made it, what they tried to do, and whether it was allowed. In production, audit logs must be enabled on the API server and shipped to a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system. They are the evidence you need after a security incident to answer "what did the attacker access and when?" — and they are also invaluable for discovering overly broad permissions that are being exercised in practice.

Understanding RBAC error messages is a skill: the format `"<verb> <resource> is forbidden: User \"<name>\" cannot <verb> resource \"<resource>\"..."` tells you exactly what rule is missing, making the fix straightforward once you understand the four RBAC objects.

**Check if a subject can perform an action:**

```bash
# Can the current user list pods in default namespace?
kubectl auth can-i list pods

# Can a specific service account list secrets?
kubectl auth can-i list secrets \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:production:my-app \
  -n production

# Can a user delete deployments?
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments \
  --as=alice@company.com \
  -n staging

# List ALL permissions for a service account:
kubectl auth can-i --list \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default
```

**Find which roles grant a specific permission:**

```bash
# Who can list secrets in the monitoring namespace?
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings \
  -n monitoring \
  -o custom-columns='KIND:.kind,NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].name'

# Get all ClusterRoles that mention secrets
kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml | grep -A5 'secrets'

# Use rbac-lookup (third-party tool) if available
# kubectl rbac-lookup serviceaccount:my-app -n production
```

**Common RBAC errors:**

```
Error: pods is forbidden: User "alice" cannot list resource "pods" in API group ""...
→ Missing get/list permission on pods

Error: cannot get resource "secrets" in API group "" in the namespace "production"
→ Missing get permission on secrets

Error: Forbidden (user=system:anonymous...)
→ Request not authenticated at all — missing token/cert
```

**Kubernetes audit log (if enabled):**

```bash
# On k3s, audit logs go to /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# Each entry shows: who, what verb, on what resource, was it allowed
# Example:
{
  "user": {"username": "system:serviceaccount:default:my-app"},
  "verb": "get",
  "objectRef": {"resource": "secrets", "namespace": "production", "name": "db-creds"},
  "responseStatus": {"code": 403}  ← denied
}
```

sections.title: Exercise: create least-privilege RBAC for a service account
sections.body:
## Hands-on: building a least-privilege ServiceAccount from scratch

This exercise follows the correct production workflow for creating RBAC: start with no permissions, identify exactly what is needed, grant precisely that, and verify both that the allowed operations work and that denied operations are blocked.

A monitoring agent is a good example because its requirements are concrete and bounded: it needs to read pod metadata and logs to discover services and scrape metrics, but it must never be able to modify workloads, read application secrets, or operate outside its designated namespace. Implementing this correctly is the difference between a monitoring tool that improves cluster observability and one that becomes a lateral movement vector if compromised.

As you work through the steps, notice how `kubectl auth can-i --list` gives you a complete view of what a ServiceAccount can and cannot do. In production, this command is your audit tool — run it against every application ServiceAccount periodically to detect **permission drift**: cases where a ServiceAccount has accumulated more access than it needs over time due to copy-pasted RBAC or emergency changes that were never cleaned up.

```bash
# ── 1. Create a ServiceAccount ────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl create serviceaccount monitoring-agent -n learning

# ── 2. Check current permissions (should be minimal) ─────────────────────
kubectl auth can-i list pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent \
  -n learning
# Expected: no

# ── 3. Create a Role for the agent ───────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: learning
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["services", "endpoints", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "replicasets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
EOF

# ── 4. Bind the Role ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: learning
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitoring-agent
  namespace: learning
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: monitoring-agent
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# ── 5. Verify permissions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Should succeed:
kubectl auth can-i list pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent -n learning

kubectl auth can-i get pods/log \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent -n learning

# Should be denied:
kubectl auth can-i delete pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent -n learning

kubectl auth can-i create secrets \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent -n learning

kubectl auth can-i list pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent -n kube-system  # different namespace

# ── 6. Inspect what the agent can do ─────────────────────────────────────
kubectl auth can-i --list \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:learning:monitoring-agent \
  -n learning

# ── 7. View the role ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl describe role monitoring-agent -n learning
kubectl describe rolebinding monitoring-agent -n learning

# ── 8. Clean up ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete rolebinding monitoring-agent -n learning
kubectl delete role monitoring-agent -n learning
kubectl delete serviceaccount monitoring-agent -n learning
```

questions.q: What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
options: A Role has more permissions than a ClusterRole
A Role is namespaced; a ClusterRole is cluster-scoped and can also be used as a namespace role template
ClusterRoles can only be bound with ClusterRoleBindings
Roles support more verbs than ClusterRoles
questions.explanation: A Role grants permissions within a single namespace. A ClusterRole grants permissions cluster-wide (for cluster-scoped resources like nodes) AND can also be bound within a namespace via a RoleBinding, making it a reusable template.

questions.q: A pod needs to read a ConfigMap named 'app-config' in the same namespace. What is the most secure way to grant this?
options: Bind cluster-admin to the pod's ServiceAccount
Use the default ServiceAccount which already has read access
Create a Role with get on configmaps with resourceNames: [app-config] and bind it to the pod's ServiceAccount
Mount the ConfigMap directly as a volume instead
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege says to grant only what's needed. A Role scoped to the specific ConfigMap name (using resourceNames) and bound to the pod's dedicated ServiceAccount is the most secure approach. The default ServiceAccount has no extra permissions by default.

questions.q: What does `kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:my-app -n prod` check?
options: Whether the current user can impersonate my-app
Whether the my-app ServiceAccount in the prod namespace can list secrets in the prod namespace
Whether secrets exist in the prod namespace
Whether my-app has a valid JWT token
questions.explanation: The --as flag impersonates another identity for the purpose of the authorization check. This command checks if the ServiceAccount named my-app in the prod namespace has permission to list secrets in the prod namespace.

sections.title: Challenge: lock down the default namespace
sections.goal: The default namespace has been running with overly broad access. Create a ServiceAccount named 'web-app-sa' in the default namespace. Grant it permission to only: get/list pods and get configmaps. Verify it cannot create pods, access secrets, or act outside the default namespace.
hints: Create the ServiceAccount first with kubectl create serviceaccount
Write a Role with two rules blocks: one for pods verbs [get, list] and one for configmaps verbs [get]
Test with: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web-app-sa
success_criteria: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web-app-sa -n default → yes
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web-app-sa -n default → no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web-app-sa -n default → no
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:web-app-sa -n kube-system → no
